node.label: Stuart Hall
node.date_label: 1973: Encoding and Decoding in the Television Discourse (CCCS paper) · 1980: Cultural Studies: Two Paradigms · 1990: Cultural Identity and Diaspora (in Identity, edited by Jonathan Rutherford)
node.description: A Jamaican-British cultural theorist of media, power and diasporic identity. His encoding/decoding analysis separates production from reception, while his identity essay treats historical rupture and difference as constitutive rather than incidental.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Encoding and Decoding in the Television Discourse (CCCS paper) (1973); Cultural Studies: Two Paradigms (1980); Cultural Identity and Diaspora (in Identity, edited by Jonathan Rutherford) (1990).

proposed_edges.relationship: Analyzes how institutional production and unequal social positions allow differently coded readings of media.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own 1973 paper pp. 1–3 and 16–18 read; encoding and decoding are distinct determinate moments. The early paper’s professional-code position and the later revision remain distinct.

proposed_edges.relationship: Treats diasporic identity as historically produced positioning, transformation and difference, alongside the political force of recovery.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own essay pp. 222–226 read in the qualified scan witness. Hall recognizes the resistance value of recovery while rejecting an eternally unchanged essence; no identity-history founding claim follows.
